questions.stem: Which statement is part of the kinetic particle model of matter?
options: Particles expand in size as the temperature of matter rises
Matter is continuous, with no spaces between its particles
Matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion
Particles of a solid are stationary until the solid is heated
questions.explanation: The kinetic particle model says all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving randomly, with spaces between them and forces acting between them. Particles in a solid still vibrate about fixed positions, and heating makes the particles move faster, not grow larger.

questions.stem: In terms of the kinetic particle model, what does the temperature of a substance measure?
options: The amount of heat stored inside the substance
The potential energy stored between its particles
The average kinetic energy of its particles
The total kinetic energy of all of its particles
questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles is the internal energy, which also depends on how many particles there are.

questions.stem: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
options: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles
The average kinetic energy of the particles in the system
The energy transferred into the system by a temperature difference
The energy the system has because of its motion as a whole
questions.explanation: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of all the particles in a system. The average kinetic energy of the particles is what temperature measures, and the energy transferred because of a temperature difference is heat.

questions.stem: A student writes that a cup of hot soup 'contains a lot of heat'. Why is this wording incorrect in physics?
options: Heat is only present when a substance is changing state, which the soup is not doing
Heat describes the kinetic energy of the soup's particles, not their potential energy
Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, not energy an object holds
Heat is the same quantity as temperature, so the soup only contains a high temperature
questions.explanation: In physics, heat is energy in transit from a hotter body to a cooler one. What the soup has is internal energy (the kinetic and potential energy of its particles) and a high temperature. Heat and temperature are different quantities.

questions.stem: A cup of coffee is at 80 °C and a backyard swimming pool is at 25 °C. Which statement about them is correct?
options: The coffee and the pool have equal internal energy because both are liquid water
The pool has more internal energy and its particles have a higher average kinetic energy
The pool has more internal energy, but its particles have a lower average kinetic energy
The coffee has more internal energy because its particles have a higher average kinetic energy
questions.explanation: The coffee's higher temperature means its particles have a higher average kinetic energy. Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles, and the pool holds vastly more particles, so its internal energy is far greater despite its lower temperature.

questions.stem: How is thermal energy transferred by conduction through a solid?
options: Particles from the hot end travel through the solid and collect at the cold end
Vibrating particles pass energy to neighbouring particles through collisions
Warmer regions of the solid flow towards cooler regions and carry energy with them
Energy is carried across the solid only by infrared waves between its particles
questions.explanation: In conduction, faster-vibrating particles collide with their neighbours and pass on kinetic energy, and in metals free electrons also carry energy quickly. A solid's particles stay in place, so there is no bulk flow, which is convection in fluids.

questions.stem: Which method of heat transfer can occur through a vacuum?
options: Radiation
Convection
Conduction
Evaporation
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers energy as electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared for everyday objects, and needs no medium. Conduction and convection both need particles, so they cannot occur in a vacuum. This is how energy from the Sun reaches Earth.

questions.stem: Split-system air conditioners are usually mounted high on a wall. Why does this help cool a whole room?
options: Walls conduct heat more slowly near the ceiling than near the floor
Cold air radiates energy downwards more strongly from a high place
Cooled air is denser, so it sinks and sets up convection currents
Cooled air is less dense, so it rises and spreads across the ceiling
questions.explanation: Air cooled by the unit becomes denser than the surrounding air and sinks, while warmer, less dense air rises to replace it. This circulation, a convection current, mixes the air in the room. Warm air rises; cool air sinks.

questions.stem: Water can be boiled in a paper cup held over a campfire without the cup catching fire. What is the best explanation?
options: The water conducts energy away from the paper, keeping it near 100 °C, below its ignition temperature
The paper reflects all of the fire's radiation, so none of the energy reaches the paper itself
The water's high latent heat stops any energy reaching the paper until the water has boiled away
Paper is a good conductor of heat, so energy passes straight through it without warming it at all
questions.explanation: Energy reaching the paper is conducted into the water, which has a high specific heat capacity and cannot rise above 100 °C while it boils. The wet paper stays near that temperature, well below the temperature at which paper ignites. Once the water is gone, the paper soon burns.

questions.stem: Why do you feel colder in wet clothes than in dry clothes on a windy day?
options: Water raises the specific heat capacity of your skin
The wind blows cold water particles into your skin
Evaporating water takes its latent heat from your body
Wet fabric reflects your body's infrared radiation away
questions.explanation: For water to evaporate, its molecules need energy equal to the latent heat of vaporisation, and much of it comes from your body. The fastest molecules escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of what remains. Wind speeds up evaporation, so you cool faster.

questions.stem: What is a temperature of −40 °C in kelvin? Use TK = TC + 273.
questions.explanation: TK = −40 + 273 = 233 K. Adding 40 instead of subtracting gives 313 K. The kelvin scale has no negative temperatures, because 0 K is absolute zero.

questions.stem: The temperature of a liquid rises from 18 °C to 33 °C. What is its change in temperature in kelvin?
questions.explanation: A kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree, so a change of 15 °C is a change of 15 K. Adding 273 is needed only for converting a single temperature reading, not a temperature difference. In Q = mcΔT the change is the same in either scale.

questions.stem: Why is the kelvin scale, rather than the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale, used as an absolute temperature scale?
options: Its zero is the freezing point of pure water at sea level
Its degrees are larger, so readings are easier to compare
It was the first temperature scale ever to be developed
Its zero is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature
questions.explanation: Zero kelvin is absolute zero, where the particles have their minimum possible kinetic energy, so temperatures in kelvin are proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles. The zero of the Celsius scale is the freezing point of water, and a kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree.

questions.stem: What is the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The energy needed to change 1 kg of it from solid to liquid
The total energy a 1 kg sample of it can store at room temperature
The temperature rise produced when 1 J is added to any mass of it
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 K
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity, c, is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1 °C), measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The energy needed to change state without a temperature change is the specific latent heat.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 15 °C to 65 °C? Use c = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Q = mcΔT = 2.0 × 4.18 × 10³ × 50 = 4.18 × 10⁵ J. Using the final temperature, 65 °C, instead of the change gives 5.43 × 10⁵ J, and leaving out the temperature change gives 8.36 × 10³ J.

questions.stem: A 0.40 kg block of ice is cooled from −5 °C to −20 °C in a freezer. How much energy is removed from it? Use c(ice) = 2.05 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The temperature change is 15 K, so Q = mcΔT = 0.40 × 2.05 × 10³ × 15 = 1.23 × 10⁴ J. Using 25 K, from adding the two temperatures, gives 2.05 × 10⁴ J, and using the specific heat capacity of water gives 2.51 × 10⁴ J.

questions.stem: Supplying 9.0 × 10³ J of energy to a 0.50 kg metal block raises its temperature by 20 K. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
options: 3.6 × 10² J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
9.0 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
2.3 × 10² J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
9.0 × 10² J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
questions.explanation: c = Q/(mΔT) = 9.0 × 10³ / (0.50 × 20) = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, close to the value for aluminium. Multiplying by the mass instead of dividing gives about 2.3 × 10² J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.stem: Why is water well suited for use as the coolant in a car engine's cooling system?
options: It has a high specific heat capacity
It has a low specific heat capacity
It has a low boiling point at normal pressure
It conducts heat better than any metal
questions.explanation: Water's high specific heat capacity means each kilogram absorbs a lot of energy for a small rise in temperature, so it can carry a lot of energy away from the engine. A low specific heat capacity would make it heat up quickly and carry little energy.

questions.stem: A student supplies energy Q to a fixed mass of water and records its temperature change ΔT for several values of Q. What graph of Q against ΔT is expected?
options: A curve that levels off as the water's temperature rises
A horizontal line, because c is constant for water
A straight line through the origin, with gradient equal to mc
A straight line through the origin, with gradient equal to 1/(mc)
questions.explanation: Since Q = mcΔT and m and c are constant, Q is directly proportional to ΔT, giving a straight line through the origin with gradient mc. A gradient of 1/(mc) would come from plotting ΔT against Q.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a 50 W heater runs for 300 s inside a 1.0 kg metal block, and the block's temperature rises by 16.5 K. The calculated specific heat capacity is about 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, but the accepted value is 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What most likely explains the difference?
options: The thermometer read too high throughout, so every temperature reading was larger than it should be
Some of the heater's energy was lost to the surroundings, so the measured temperature rise was too small
The block absorbed energy from the surroundings, so the measured temperature rise was too large
The heater supplied more energy than its rating, so the energy used in the calculation was too large
questions.explanation: c = Q/(mΔT) = 15 000/(1.0 × 16.5) ≈ 909 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Energy lost to the air means less than 15 000 J went into the block, so ΔT was smaller and the calculated c too large. A constant offset in the thermometer cancels out when the change is calculated.

questions.stem: While ice melts at 0 °C, energy is still being added, but the temperature stays constant. In terms of the kinetic particle model, why?
options: The energy escapes to the surroundings as fast as it is added, so none stays in the ice
The energy is stored as extra mass in the water particles as the ice turns to liquid
The energy increases the particles' potential energy as bonds break, not their kinetic energy
The energy increases the particles' kinetic energy, but some particles leave as vapour
questions.explanation: During a change of state the added energy works against the forces between particles, increasing their potential energy, so the internal energy rises while the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, does not change.

questions.stem: What is the specific latent heat of a substance?
options: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of it with no temperature change
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by exactly 1 K
The temperature at which 1 kg of the substance changes from solid to liquid
The energy stored in 1 kg of the substance at its boiling temperature
questions.explanation: Specific latent heat, L, is the energy absorbed or released per kilogram when a substance changes state at constant temperature, so Q = mL. Latent heat of fusion applies to melting and freezing, and latent heat of vaporisation to boiling and condensing.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to melt 0.25 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C? Use L(fusion) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Q = mL = 0.25 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 8.35 × 10⁴ J. No temperature change is involved because the ice is already at its melting point. Dividing L by the mass instead gives 1.34 × 10⁶ J.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to turn 0.10 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 20 °C? Use c(ice) = 2.05 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c(water) = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L(fusion) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Warm the ice: 0.10 × 2.05 × 10³ × 10 = 2050 J. Melt it: 0.10 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 33 400 J. Warm the water: 0.10 × 4.18 × 10³ × 20 = 8360 J. The total is 4.38 × 10⁴ J. Leaving out the first stage gives 4.18 × 10⁴ J, and leaving out the melting stage gives about 1.04 × 10⁴ J.

questions.stem: A constant-power heater warms a sample of water from liquid to steam. Why is the temperature-time graph steeper for the steam than for the liquid water?
options: Steam has a higher specific heat capacity than liquid water
Steam absorbs latent heat as it warms, so it needs less energy
Steam is less dense, so the heater supplies it with more power
Steam has a lower specific heat capacity than liquid water
questions.explanation: With constant power, the rate of temperature rise is P/(mc). Steam's specific heat capacity (about 2.00 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is about half that of water (4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), so its temperature rises about twice as fast. Latent heat is absorbed only during the change of state, on the flat section.

questions.stem: Steam at 100 °C condenses on a person's skin and the water cools to 40 °C. How much energy does 0.010 kg of steam give to the skin? Use L(vaporisation) = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ and c(water) = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Condensing: 0.010 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 22 600 J. Cooling from 100 °C to 40 °C: 0.010 × 4.18 × 10³ × 60 = 2508 J. The total is about 2.51 × 10⁴ J, which is why steam burns are worse than burns from water at the same temperature. Using a 40 K change instead of 60 K gives 2.43 × 10⁴ J.

questions.stem: Two objects in contact are in thermal equilibrium. Which statement is true?
options: They are both at room temperature, as all objects eventually are
They are at the same temperature, so there is no net heat transfer
They have the same internal energy, so no energy can pass between them
They have the same mass and specific heat capacity as each other
questions.explanation: Objects in thermal equilibrium are at the same temperature, so the average kinetic energy of their particles is the same and there is no net transfer of heat. Their internal energies can differ greatly, for example if one is much larger.

questions.stem: A hot metal block at 90 °C is placed in water at 20 °C in an insulated container. Once thermal equilibrium is reached, which statement is correct?
options: The water's temperature has risen by exactly as much as the block's temperature has fallen
The block has lost all of its thermal energy to the water, which now holds all of the energy
Both are at the same temperature, and their particles have the same average kinetic energy
Both have the same internal energy, because energy flowed until it was shared out equally
questions.explanation: Energy flows from the block to the water until their temperatures are equal, at which point the average kinetic energy of the particles is the same in both. The temperature changes are equal only if the two have equal values of mc, which is generally not true.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg copper block (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is placed in 0.20 kg of water (c = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 20 °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
questions.explanation: Energy lost by copper = energy gained by water: 0.50 × 390 × (100 − T) = 0.20 × 4180 × (T − 20), so 195(100 − T) = 836(T − 20) and T ≈ 35 °C. Averaging the two temperatures gives 60 °C, and swapping the specific heat capacities gives about 97 °C.

questions.stem: How much ice at 0 °C must be added to 0.30 kg of water at 25 °C so that the mixture just reaches 0 °C with all the ice melted? Use c(water) = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L(fusion) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Assume no energy is exchanged with the surroundings.
questions.explanation: Energy released by the water cooling to 0 °C: 0.30 × 4180 × 25 = 31 350 J. This melts m = 31 350 / 3.34 × 10⁵ ≈ 0.094 kg of ice. Leaving out the 0.30 kg mass of water gives 0.31 kg, and using the latent heat of vaporisation gives 0.014 kg.

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C. The theoretical final temperature is 44 °C, but a student measures 41 °C. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |measured − theoretical| / theoretical × 100% = 3/44 × 100% ≈ 6.8%. Dividing by the measured value, 41 °C, gives 7.3%. The result is low because some energy was lost to the surroundings and the container.

questions.stem: A cup of hot tea cools in a room, but the room never spontaneously heats the tea back up. Which law of thermodynamics describes this?
options: The first law: heat flows spontaneously from colder to hotter
The second law: heat flows spontaneously from hotter to colder
The first law: energy cannot be created or destroyed
The second law: internal energy always stays constant
questions.explanation: The second law of thermodynamics says heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder one, never the reverse. The first law, conservation of energy, would allow energy to flow either way, so it cannot explain the direction.

questions.stem: In the first law of thermodynamics, ΔU = Q + W, what does W represent?
options: The work done on the system
The work done by the system
The energy wasted as heat
The power supplied to the system
questions.explanation: In the form ΔU = Q + W, Q is the energy added to the system by heating and W is the work done on the system. Work done by the system, such as a gas expanding against a piston, counts as negative W. The law is a statement of conservation of energy.

questions.stem: How can a system with thermal energy do mechanical work?
options: A heated solid stores extra mass, which then falls to do work
Heat flows directly into kinetic energy with no losses at all
A heated liquid gives off radiation that turns the engine's gears
A heated gas expands and pushes a piston, as in a steam engine
questions.explanation: Heating a gas increases the speed of its particles, which push harder on their container. If one wall is a movable piston, the expanding gas does work on it. Steam engines and internal combustion engines both work this way, and some energy is always lost as heat.

questions.stem: A gas absorbs 600 J of heat and does 250 J of work on its surroundings as it expands. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q + W, where Q = +600 J and the work done on the gas is W = −250 J. So ΔU = 600 − 250 = +350 J. Adding the 250 J gives 850 J, which treats the work as being done on the gas.

questions.stem: A gas is compressed, with 400 J of work done on it, while it loses 150 J of heat to the surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q + W = (−150) + (+400) = +250 J. Work done on the gas adds energy, and heat lost removes energy. Treating both as gains gives 550 J.

questions.stem: A gas in a cylinder expands, doing 300 J of work on a piston, and its internal energy decreases by 100 J. What heat transfer occurred?
options: 400 J of heat was added to the gas
200 J of heat was lost by the gas
400 J of heat was lost by the gas
200 J of heat was added to the gas
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q + W, with ΔU = −100 J and W = −300 J (work done by the gas). So −100 = Q − 300, giving Q = +200 J: the gas absorbed 200 J of heat. It lost more energy by doing work than it gained by heating.

questions.stem: Energy transfers in mechanical systems always reduce the amount of useable energy. Why?
options: Some energy always stays locked inside the machine forever
Some energy always becomes heat that spreads into the surroundings
Some energy is always destroyed by friction between moving parts
Some energy is always turned into mass as the parts move
questions.explanation: Friction, air resistance and electrical resistance transform some energy into thermal energy, which spreads into the environment and cannot easily be used again. The energy is not destroyed, as conservation of energy still holds; it just becomes less useful.

questions.stem: An engine takes in 2.5 × 10⁴ J of energy from burning fuel and does 7.5 × 10³ J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: η = energy output / energy input × 100% = 7.5 × 10³ / 2.5 × 10⁴ × 100% = 30%. The other 70% of the energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat. Dividing the input by the output gives a value above 100%, which is impossible.

questions.stem: A 2000 W electric kettle runs for 150 s and heats 0.80 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. What is the kettle's efficiency? Use c = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Energy into the water: Q = 0.80 × 4.18 × 10³ × 80 = 267 520 J. Energy supplied: 2000 × 150 = 300 000 J. η = 267 520 / 300 000 × 100% ≈ 89%. Inverting the ratio gives 112%, which is impossible for any real device.
